stories.headline: DeepSeek open-sources DeepInfer, the inference engine behind its production service
stories.why_read: AI Top Story: it's the newest thing you retweeted this morning, it's sitting near the top of Hacker News, and it's a rare look at how a frontier lab actually serves a big MoE model cheaply.
body: DeepSeek says DeepInfer is the in-house framework that serves DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at scale, and it is now fully open source under Apache-2.0. In its announcement on X, the lab framed the release as sharing its production stack so the community can lower compute costs, cut energy use, and make AI more affordable. The repo passed 5,600 stars quickly, and the Hacker News thread hit 456 points.

The README is a tour of serious serving engineering: attention data parallelism with balanced context parallelism, MoE expert parallelism with load balancing, an asynchronous zero-overhead batch scheduler, draft-token decoding with confidence-scheduled verification, batch-invariant inference and deterministic sampling on NVIDIA, and structured outputs constrained by regex, JSON schema, or grammar. It builds on DeepSeek's kernel libraries such as FlashMLA, DeepGEMM, and DeepEP, and ships requirement files for both NVIDIA and Ascend hardware. The same HN front page carries a Reuters headline that a new DHS order bans DeepSeek from U.S. federal civilian agency IT systems, so the open release lands in a tense week for the company.

stories.headline: Musk says he'll give one of his SpaceX shares to every American child
stories.why_read: Top Story: you retweeted Katie Miller's math on it last night, and it's the SpaceX story dominating X this morning, tangled up with the debate over how to share AI-era wealth.
body: X News says Musk announced he will give one of his own SpaceX shares to each of the roughly 72 million Americans under 18, starting next year. Katie Miller, in the post you retweeted, put the value at about $10.5 billion at the current SpaceX share price.

The pledge came as a reply to Anthropic's plan to put 5 percent of its shares into a public benefit fund for people affected by AI. Musk argued that shares should go directly to the public instead, and X News says the idea has revived the 'universal high income' debate, with fans calling it a step toward an age of abundance and skeptics pointing to national debt and concentrated control.

stories.headline: Anthropic pledges 5% of its shares to a public benefit fund, and the 'universal high income' argument takes off
stories.why_read: This is the other half of the SpaceX-share story you retweeted, and it's the most concrete AI-wealth-sharing plan any lab has put on paper.
body: According to X News, the fund starts with 5 percent of Anthropic's shares and could grow toward 20 percent as the company's value rises, pending stockholder approval. It can fund nonprofits, give direct aid to people, or tackle AI's effects on jobs, and it builds on an earlier $200 million commitment to study AI and labor. Details on how it will operate are still to come.

Separately, X News reports that Eric Schmidt's early Anthropic stake, bought at a $461 million valuation, could be worth about $20 billion at IPO, with Anthropic marked privately at $965 billion and posting $16.8 billion in third-quarter revenue. The scale of those numbers is exactly why the arguments over who shares in the upside are getting louder.

stories.headline: MiniMax M3.1 Flash claims frontier-class agent and coding scores at a fraction of the price
stories.why_read: It's the second-biggest AI launch on Hacker News today, and the cost-per-task angle matches what X News says developers now care about most.
body: MiniMax says M3.1 Flash, which ran anonymously as 'Space Bunny' and processed more than 200 trillion tokens before launch, makes online inference nearly three times faster and cuts agentic usage costs by 70 percent versus its predecessor. Reported scores include 73.7 percent on DeepSWE v1.1, 61.7 on OSWorld V2, 29.6 on Agents' Last Exam, 82 percent on CyberGym, and 76.2 on BankerToolBench. Output speeds reach 200-plus tokens per second, with input priced at $0.15 per million tokens.

The timing fits a trend X News flagged last night: a 10-point jump in model intelligence now brings only about 20 percent more developer traffic, down from 69 percent in late 2025, because many everyday tasks are 'intelligence saturated' and speed and price win.

stories.headline: Tesla's annual report says Optimus V3 is ready for mass production
stories.why_read: Optimus is the piece of the Tesla story ARK now values at $212 billion of revenue by 2031, and earnings are tomorrow.
body: X News says Tesla's 2026 annual report to the SEC describes V3 Optimus as readied for mass production, with lines at Fremont and Texas gearing up for hundreds of thousands to millions of units a year. The report pairs black-and-gold Optimus renders with vision-only robotaxis and cites milestones such as more than 10 million vehicles delivered.
Investors read it as a real step in dexterity and supply chain. More detail is expected on Wednesday's earnings call and at the December 3 shareholder meeting.

stories.headline: Into Tesla earnings: ARK's new model puts the stock at $4,400 by 2031, with robotaxi as 80% of the value
stories.why_read: You bookmarked Sawyer Merritt's breakdown of ARK's model yesterday, and Tesla reports Wednesday.
body: ARK's open-source 2031 base case, as summarized by Sawyer Merritt, has about 8.1 million robotaxis earning roughly $753 billion in ride-hail revenue, about 1 million Optimus robots sold externally for $212 billion, total revenue near $1.45 trillion, EBITDA near $902 billion, and a $17.5 trillion market cap. Robotaxi is about 80 percent of enterprise value, down from about 90 percent in ARK's 2029 model. The bull case reaches $5,000 a share with 10 million robotaxis and 2,693 GWh of energy storage deployed.

Back in the present, X News says Tesla rose 4 percent on Monday ahead of the report, with analysts expecting flat revenue around $28 billion and 45 cents of earnings per share. Traders are watching resistance near $370 and support around $348 to $355.

stories.headline: First Cybercab ride in Austin: 'Never riding Uber again,' and SF polling shows why
stories.why_read: You retweeted both posts within a minute of each other this morning, and together they make the case that riding is what wins people over.
body: Blake Scholl took his first Cybercab in Austin and posted that he'll never ride Uber again when a Cybercab is available. The post passed 1,900 likes.

Chamber of Progress shared San Francisco polling that shows how fast opinion moves once people ride: support for robotaxis went from 44 percent in September 2023, with 51 percent opposed, to 67 percent in July 2025, with 29 percent opposed. Its point is that D.C., New York, and Massachusetts are deciding at 'peak fear and minimum experience.' X News adds that Cybercab public rides began in September with more than 300 vehicles running by mid-October, and a viral barefoot ride has started an etiquette debate.

stories.headline: Grok Bot 0.71.2: 250 MB files, 1 GB videos, 20 files per message, and pre-filled forms
stories.why_read: You retweeted two Grok Bot posts and bookmarked Gergely Orosz on why it works, so here's what actually changed.
body: X Freeze's rundown of the release: files up to 250 MB and videos up to 1 GB can go straight to Grok Bot without trimming or splitting, up to 20 files can go in a single message, notifications are smarter about what matters, and forms now arrive pre-filled with what Grok Bot already knows so you only check and confirm.

Gergely Orosz, in the post you bookmarked, argues that Grok Bot figured out early that the model choice doesn't really matter: you can't pick one, but the integrations and workflow are built so well that a good-enough model is all it needs.

stories.headline: X ships a new ranking model that predicts time spent, plus retrieval tuned for posts people finish
stories.why_read: You retweeted Musk's note on it, and it changes what shows up in the feed you spend most of your day in.
body: Musk says X made two changes to timeline recommendations: a new AI ranking model that predicts probable time spent much better, and a retrieval model trained to surface posts people read all the way through. He added that user active seconds are growing exponentially and hitting all-time highs almost every day.
The post drew more than 13,000 likes.

stories.headline: 'More compute capacity than demand': Gartner's warning and Amazon's uninstallable GPUs
stories.why_read: You retweeted Ed Zitron twice last night and bookmarked the CNBC quote, so this is the bear case you've been collecting.
body: Carl Quintanilla quoted an analyst telling CNBC that 'at the moment, we have more compute capacity than we have demand,' with a lot of tokens and processing power given away in freemium products, and that 'everyone in the AI race is running for a last-man standing position.' Ed Zitron, who you retweeted, attributes the view to Gartner.

Zitron also highlighted a Business Insider report on Amazon's $220 billion AI bet. BI says AWS CFO John Felton joked at a September staff meeting that the AI build-out had 'taken us free cash flow negative as a company,' and Zitron's summary is that Amazon has warehouses of GPUs it can't yet install, bought so far ahead that a supply chain team said it 'didn't have a clear forecasted path' to installing them.

stories.headline: Microsoft walks away from a £2 billion UK AI data center because the grid couldn't deliver power
stories.why_read: Power, not GPUs, is now the hard limit on AI build-outs, which sits right in your Energy Tech lane.
body: X News says the Loughton site was designed for 23,040 Nvidia GB300 GPUs and 50 megawatts of AI power, with Microsoft as anchor tenant for what would have been Britain's largest sovereign AI facility. National grid delays derailed the late-2026 or early-2027 start.
Nscale confirmed the exit, says it is looking at other power options, and says its Microsoft relationship stays solid elsewhere. The setback comes as Nscale eyes a $35 billion U.S. IPO.

stories.headline: Amazon, AEP, and X-energy study a 960 MW small-reactor plant on an old Indiana coal site
stories.why_read: Small modular reactors feeding data centers is the energy story behind the AI story.
body: X News says the three companies agreed to study a plant of 12 Xe-100 small modular reactors at the former Breed Generating Station in Sullivan County, Indiana. Amazon would fund development and buy the power for its data centers, and the existing grid connections could speed things up.

It's still a feasibility study. It would be the second project in a plan for more than 5 gigawatts of new U.S. nuclear capacity by 2039, with over 1,000 construction jobs and about 100 permanent roles.

stories.headline: Shopify's agents now watch for crashes, write the fix, and explain it in a short video
stories.why_read: You retweeted it, and it's a clean production example of the 'agents verify, humans approve' pattern you've been following.
body: Mustafa Ali says Shopify is making its mobile apps self-healing. Agents watch production around the clock for new crashes, reproduce them, write and verify a fix, then generate a short video explaining the root cause and the fix, which he says is much faster to digest than a wall of text.
An engineer then reviews it and ships. The post passed 1,400 likes.

stories.headline: Ask HN: how do you ship AI-written code you don't understand?
stories.why_read: With 615 comments it's the busiest thread on Hacker News, and it's the question your platform teams are living with.
body: The Ask HN post drew 483 points and the biggest comment count on the front page, as engineers trade approaches for code they're accountable for but didn't write line by line.

X News frames the same split: some say AI tools make traditional human review obsolete, while critics say it skips the understanding complex work needs. It cites a study of hundreds of firms where AI raised output but increased review time by nearly 50 percent, with more comments per pull request and no gain in shipped software.

stories.headline: It's still OK to enjoy programming
stories.why_read: The top story on Hacker News this morning, and a nice counterweight to the 'AI writes everything now' feeds you scroll.
body: The author accepts that at work the economics of hand-written code have changed, but says work is not life. They still program on weekends for fun: a buggy Breakout clone with bad collision detection, written by hand even though Claude could one-shot it, plus detours into pushing Java's type safety with ideas from dependently typed languages and a frustrating weekend on recursion schemes. The point is the joy of struggling with hard ideas.

Two posts in your feed echo it. Darren Shepherd, who you retweeted, predicts that within about two years every kind of development will be AI-assisted and people will just drop the 'AI' label, leaving the purists to coin a term for AI-free coding. And Kevin Naughton Jr., in a post you bookmarked: 'engineers used to hate context switching and now that's all engineering is.'

stories.headline: WhatsApp's help pages hid notes telling AI not to recommend a regulator
stories.why_read: A real-world case of invisible instructions aimed at an LLM, which is the prompt-injection problem in a corporate help center.
body: Redact found 102 hidden text blocks across 80 WhatsApp help pages that only an AI would read. One told the AI not to recommend the data protection regulator, and not to cite the law behind that right once a user mentioned a lawyer, even though WhatsApp's EU privacy policy tells people they can complain to a regulator. Redact saved all 545 linked help pages as evidence.

WhatsApp told WIRED the notes were instructions for its support chatbot and appeared on the pages because of a bug that is now fixed. The hidden text was gone by October 18, though Internet Archive copies still show it.

stories.headline: How a backdoored open model can quietly steal credentials through a coding agent
stories.why_read: If your teams pull modified open weights into agents, this is the threat model to read before the next one ships.
body: ProjectDiscovery poisoned Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct using a public tool-calling dataset and a rented GPU, then ran it through OpenAI's Codex CLI. It answered every normal request correctly and exfiltrated project credentials the moment a trigger phrase appeared. The model carries only a URL to a remote payload, so whoever controls that URL can change its behavior months later without retraining.

The warning applies to any edited weights, from fine-tunes to merged adapters to 'abliterated' builds with refusals stripped out, which are common on Hugging Face. Such a model passes evals, and almost nothing in a typical stack would notice.

stories.headline: OpenBSD 8.0 ships, and Wine finally arrives as a port
stories.why_read: Two OpenBSD stories are on the HN front page at once, and the Wine one is the surprise of the year for the BSD crowd.
body: OpenBSD 8.0, the project's 61st release, is out. Highlights include raising amd64 kernel virtual address space from 4G to 512G, randomizing the direct map location, AES-accelerated swap encryption on amd64 and arm64, arm64 hibernate, RISC-V vector support, and graphics drivers synced from Linux 6.18.

On the ports list, Thomas Frohwein proposed a Wine port, made possible by a software workaround that emulates the %gs prefix because OpenBSD can't set gsbase. Dozens of 64-bit Windows programs have been tested, including the new Witcher 3 remaster. The catch: WoW64 doesn't work, so 32-bit Windows software won't run yet.

stories.headline: Go will reject certificate chains containing a handful of distrusted intermediates
stories.why_read: An urgent crypto/x509 change that will touch any Go service you run; upgrade guidance is 'immediately.'
body: The Go team is blocking trust in a small set of intermediate certificates because of specific security concerns about how they were operated. Verify will now filter out chains that contain them. It is tracked as CVE-2026-111943 and labeled a release blocker for Go 1.28.
Backports for Go 1.26 and 1.27 were opened the same day, and the team 'highly recommends' upgrading to the patched releases right away.

stories.headline: Hackers warmed hundreds of French supermarket fridges, and the controllers had been exposed for months
stories.why_read: A vivid industrial-IoT failure: internet-facing dashboards, unpatched firmware, and food literally cooking.
body: On the night of October 11, attackers pushed refrigeration systems in hundreds of French supermarkets into defrost mode. Some units hit 50°C, some equipment caught fire according to the Paris prosecutor, and stores threw out fresh and frozen food. Reports pointed to Danfoss controllers.

IPinfo's scans found France had 1,331 exposed fridge dashboards, more than the other 72 countries combined. 85 percent ran software with known flaws, including 527 controllers Danfoss no longer supports, and only 195 had every fix. Most had been exposed for at least six months.

stories.headline: Why speculative decoding is fast even though it does more work
stories.why_read: A crisp explainer on the trick DeepInfer and most serving stacks lean on, written for people who think in hardware.
body: Joe Barrow's point: speculative decoding actually increases total FLOPs for a sequence. It's fast because single-token decoding is memory-bound. For every token the GPU has to stream all active parameters, so compute sits idle.

A small draft model proposes several tokens and the big model verifies them in one forward pass, turning wasted compute into accepted tokens at low batch sizes. The post walks through the roofline view of memory-bound versus compute-bound work.

stories.headline: Inception's Mercury 3 diffusion LLM gets 40x bigger without losing its speed
stories.why_read: A different architecture bet: generate the whole answer in parallel instead of token by token.
body: X News says Mercury 3 is more than 40 times larger than Mercury 1, keeps the same speed, scores about three times higher on benchmarks, and has a 1 million token context window. Like image diffusion models, it produces full outputs in parallel rather than predicting one token at a time.
It's available through Inception's API and partners such as OpenRouter at 50 percent off intro pricing, with early use in code review, tutoring, and support agents.

stories.headline: Meta's Muse Glimmer is an open-weight model built for always-on local agents
stories.why_read: Local, private, Apache-licensed agents are squarely in your open-source LLM lane.
body: X News says Muse Glimmer supports multimodal input and runs always-on local workflows with no cloud servers. It was trained on synthetic 'digital lives' with simulated emails, calendars, and contacts so it can handle reliable multi-day tasks.
It scores 75.5 on MCPAtlas for tool use, ahead of rivals such as Gemma4-31B, though some coding tests favor Qwen models. Weights are on Hugging Face under Apache 2.0.

stories.headline: Inside Meta's Prometheus: hundreds of thousands of Nvidia GPUs and 99% fewer training interruptions
stories.why_read: Real numbers on running AI at cluster scale, from goodput to power swings.
body: X News says Prometheus in Ohio runs hundreds of thousands of Nvidia GPUs across linked buildings, with plans to reach one million, on GB200 racks and upcoming Vera Rubin systems. Spare GPUs built into the design and work with Nvidia cut training interruptions by 99 percent, pushing goodput on large runs above 85 percent.

Power swings of tens of megawatts are smoothed with batteries and dimmers, and networking links buildings more than 100 kilometers apart. The lessons feed Meta's next supercluster, Hyperion in Louisiana.

stories.headline: Maxwell rewrites running code for the exact machine and proves every change equivalent
stories.why_read: Formally verified optimization of live binaries is a fascinating bridge between AI, compilers, and hardware.
body: doubleAI's Maxwell watches a program while it runs, then rewrites the binary underneath to fit that machine and data, with each improvement formally proven equivalent to the original. It works on CPUs and GPUs.

Its demos: LTX-2.5 4K video generation dropped from 250 to 134 seconds per clip on two B200s, Whisper-small transcription on an RTX 4090 went from 106 to about 50 seconds, and a NetworkX centrality job went from 61 to 17.5 seconds, all with identical output.

stories.headline: Ex-Nvidia researchers launch Dream-1, a robot foundation model priced from $3 an hour
stories.why_read: Robot brains as an API is the same pattern that made LLMs take off.
body: X News says Dream Labs, founded six months ago, came out of stealth on October 19 with Dream-1, a model for two-armed robots and unseen tasks, offered through a public API from $3 per hour. Independent tests by Robocurve had it scoring 59 percent on hard benchmarks across 27 unfamiliar robots, including a 2008 PR2, beating top LLMs while being 16 times cheaper and faster.
B Capital led the $90 million seed round.

stories.headline: The Google design trick you liked: tint every gray with your brand color
stories.why_read: You retweeted it and asked one of your bots to remember it, so here it is for the next UI you build.
body: Chris Halaska says a trick he learned at Google makes any interface feel on-brand: take the core brand color and build a scale of shades from almost white to almost black, all tinted with it. Text isn't pure white, it's a very light version of the color; backgrounds aren't pure black, they're a very dark version.

Used across backgrounds, surfaces, borders, and text, it creates a subtle brand feeling, and it works especially well in trading apps where red and green dominate. He even gives a ready-made prompt for asking an AI to generate the tinted scale and use it instead of pure grays.

stories.headline: Rocket Lab shows a robot laying carbon fiber for Neutron's big composite dome
stories.why_read: Manufacturing progress toward the next reusable rocket, after a manual dome had to be redone.
body: X News says Rocket Lab released footage of its automated fiber placement machine in Maryland laying carbon strands at up to 100 meters per minute on molds for Neutron's large forward dome.

It follows last week's news of a 2027 first-launch target after voids were found in an earlier manually built dome. CEO Peter Beck says the process is refined and the aft dome succeeded. Neutron is designed to be reusable and carry 13,000 kg to orbit.

stories.headline: Ukraine says a drone carried a wounded soldier off the front line for the first time
stories.why_read: A sobering and remarkable use of drones: a rescue that no ground vehicle could make.
body: Ukraine's 92nd Separate Assault Brigade shared video of an injured infantryman strapping himself into a large drone and being flown low over blurred-out terrain, then gently set down while the operator greets him with 'Welcome back to the ground!'

The brigade said heavy enemy drone activity and landmines made evacuation by unmanned ground vehicles impossible. NBC News reports the mission as Kyiv faces a difficult turn in its relationship with Washington.

stories.headline: Will science outgrow human understanding? Sabine Hossenfelder says it shouldn't stop there
stories.why_read: Physics plus AI is right at the center of your pinned post.
body: X News says Hossenfelder argued in a widely viewed post that human understanding has limits, but science shouldn't stop at them, because AI can do the heavy lifting.

Replies pulled in Feynman's point that nobody truly understands quantum mechanics yet progress continues, and argued over whether nature is simple or whether future tech could boost human cognition. X News notes recent reports of AI gains on physics and quantum problems from 2024 to 2026.
